list.listitem: Chronic serous otitis media (CSOM) is diagnosed via pneumatic otoscopy. C
The main goal of diagnosis and treatment is to identify children at risk for language delay, learning problems, or significant hearing loss. B
Drug therapy is not effective for altering the course of the disease or preventing language delay, learning problems, or significant hearing loss. A
Tympanostomy tube placement is the usual recommended treatment for children with CSOM of at least 3 months duration, although evidence of long-term, clinically meaningful benefit is modest. B

background.definition: Chronic serous otitis media (CSOM) is the presence of a seromucous exudate in the middle ear for more than 12 weeks. Despite its name, CSOM does not exhibit signs or symptoms of infection.

list.listitem: 2.2 million episodes of CSOM diagnosed annually.
Among infants to school-aged children, 90% will have at least 1 episode.

During first year of life over 50% of children, by second year of life, more than 60%. Among school-aged children, 25% have had CSOM, and among child care center attendees, approximately 50% to 60% have had it.
The point prevalence in screening studies is around 20%.
The combined direct and indirect cost of CSOM is estimated at 4.0 billion dollars annually.
Children with CSOM are at risk for speech, language, or learning developmental problems.
The conductive hearing loss that can accompany CSOM may adversely affect binaural processing, sound localization, speech perception in noise, and early language acquisition.

Children at greatest risk for these delays have permanent hearing loss independent of CSOM, speech and language delays or disorders, autism-spectrum disorder and other pervasive developmental disorders, craniofacial disorders manifested with cognitive, speech, and language delays, uncorrectable visual loss, cleft palate, and developmental delays.
Inflammatory response following acute otitis media
Eustachian tube dysfunction
Allergy
Craniofacial anomalies (cleft palate, Down's syndrome, Robin sequence, and ears with deafness)
Barotrauma
Gastroesophageal reflux
Persistent fluid in the middle ear causes decreased mobility of the tympanic membrane that serves as a barrier to sound conduction.
The effusion, which contains leukotrienes, prostaglandins, and arachidonic acid, can cause a local inflammatory response that can cause structural damage to the tympanic membrane.
Relative underventilation of the middle ear produces negative pressure, predisposing to focal retraction pockets, generalized atelectasis of the tympanic membrane, and cholesteatoma.

Spontaneous resolution is less likely when CSOM begins in the summer or fall, hearing loss greater than 30 dB HL in better-hearing ear, history of prior tympanostomy tubes, and not having an adenoidectomy.
An individual patient data meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found no evidence that antibiotics for acute otitis media prevents subsequent CSOM. A

Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine reduces the risk of acute otitis media approximately 6% (NNT = 16). However, a meta-analysis of three RCTs showed no significant preventive benefit from anti-pneumococcal vaccination in CSOM. A
Use of ventilation tubes ("grommets") reduces the likelihood of AOM in children (1.5 fewer episodes over 6 months) but is based on only 2 studies with 148 participants. B
Pneumatic otoscopy is the primary diagnostic method for CSOM. C
Tympanometry can confirm the diagnosis of CSOM. C
Hearing testing is recommended when CSOM persists for 3 months or longer, or at any time when language delay, learning problems, or a significant hearing loss is suspected in a child with CSOM. B

Forty to 50% of children with CSOM are asymptomatic. Those with symptoms may describe mild intermittent ear pain, fullness, or popping. Infants may manifest pain by ear rubbing, excessive irritability, or sleep disturbances and may not respond by turning head toward a voice or environmental sound.

Hearing loss may be suggested by a child's lack of attentiveness, behavioral changes, failure to respond to normal conversational-level speech, or needing excessively high sound levels when using audio equipment or watching television.
On examination, suspicion of fluid behind the tympanic membrane is the major factor in diagnosis; the color of the tympanic membrane is not helpful.

Pneumatic otoscopy is the primary diagnostic method for CSOM. The tympanic membrane often has impaired mobility with an air-fluid level or air bubble visible within the middle ear. The test is performed by gently inserting the speculum only into the outer one-third (cartilaginous portion) of the ear canal. Compressing the pneumatic bulb slightly before insertion of the speculum into the ear canal allows easier assessment of negative pressure within the middle ear.
Tympanometry with a standard 226-Hz probe can confirm the diagnosis of CSOM in infants 4 months or older. Infants younger than 4 months require equipment with a higher probe tone frequency.

Pure tone audiometry identifies 93.4% of children aged 3 to 16 years with hearing loss less than or equal to 20 dB. Hearing testing in children 4 years and older uses conventional audiometry with earphones at 500, 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz. Children fail if at any one hearing frequency in either ear, a loss of 20 dB or higher was recorded. Comprehensive audiologic evaluation is necessary for children failing or are younger than 4 years old. In children younger than 4 years, evaluate air-conduction and bone-conduction thresholds for pure tones, speech detection, or speech recognition.
The average hearing level associated with CSOM in children 7 months old to 12 years old is 24.5 dB (range of 10-40 dB).
Language testing for those failing the hearing test.
Transient evoked otoacoustic emissions detected 100% of hearing loss greater than or equal to 30 dB following tympanostomy tube insertion.
The main goal of diagnosis is to identify children at risk for delay in language acquisition or development.
Serous otitis media is diagnosed by persistent middle ear fluid resulting in decreased mobility of the tympanic membrane. See for a suggested approach to evaluation and management.
Child with CSOM not at risk for hearing or language delays should be managed with watchful waiting for 3 months from the date of effusion onset. C
Antihistamines and decongestants are not effective for CSOM. A
Antibiotic or corticosteroid treatment does not offer long-term efficacy. A

Tympanostomy tube insertion is the initial procedure for persistent or recurrent CSOM. Adenoidectomy plus myringotomy, with or without tympanostomy tube placement, is the appropriate repeat procedure. B

Children with persistent bilateral CSOM documented over a period of 3 months with hearing loss in the better ear of 25 to 30 dB or worse averaged for 0, 500, 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz. should be considered for placement of tympanostomy tubes. Adjuvant adenopathy not recommended without presence of persistent and/or frequent upper respiratory symptoms (NICE clinical guideline 60). C

Child with CSOM at 3 months duration not receiving tympanostomy tubes should be re-evaluated at 3- to 6-month intervals until the effusion is resolved, significant hearing loss detected, or structural abnormalities of the tympanic membrane or middle ear are suspected. C
Ventilation tube insertion reduces the symptoms of CSOM and improves the childs quality of life. B
Drug therapy does not provide lasting benefit with regard to hearing loss or language acquisition.

Acute otitis media with effusion disappeared 2 weeks earlier in children treated with 40 mg/kg amoxicillin/clavulanate for 7 days than those treated with placebo. Otoscopic findings normalize 1.4 weeks sooner in those children receiving the antibiotic.
Two weeks after tympanostomy tube placement only 5% of children receiving hydrocortisone-bacitracin-colistin eardrops had otorrhea compared to 44% of children treated with oral antibotics.

A network meta-analysis noted that a topical antibiotic-glucocorticoid drop formulation was more effective than taking an oral antibiotic in treating otorrhea and that there is no evidence that following water precautions are necessary in preventing otorrhea.
No statistical or clinical benefit is derived from antihistamines, decongestants, and antihistamine/decongestant combinations in resolving CSOM.
Systematic review of 2 randomized trials found no benefit after 3 months anti-reflux treatment.

A review of RCT's for effect of antibiotic use for CSOM did not support the routine use of antibiotics. The largest effect of using antibiotics was found in children treated continuously for four weeks and 3 months, and there was no substantial improvement in hearing or need for tympanosity tube placement. Antimicrobial therapy for 2 to 8 weeks in RCTs produce modest short-term benefit. Benefit obtained can be lost within 2 weeks of stopping antibiotics. About 7 children would need to be treated to achieve one short-term response. In an additional study children aged 3 to 14 years 72.1% of cases of early stage CSOM recovered following an 8 week course of low dose macrolide.

Oral steroids, with or without an oral antibiotic, lead to quicker resolution of CSOM in the short term, but there is no long-term benefit or evidence that hearing loss is improved. An RCT of 144 children with CSOM found that while there was a small early benefit of steroid plus amoxicillin over amoxicillin alone (NNT = 6), which disappeared at 4 weeks. A systematic review came to a similar conclusion.

A RCT of a 7-day course of oral prednisolone in children aged 2 to 8 years old found no statistically significant differences in hearing or tympanostomy tube use compared to placebo t 1, 6, and 12 months.
The use of inhaled nasal steroids in children with CSOM is not worthwhile because the NNT for a 1-month course of nasal steroids is >11.

A study randomized children with otitis media with effusion aged 2 to 11 years (n = 290) to oral steroids, oral steroids+intranasal steroids, versus watchful waiting. Resolution was faster with oral steroids at 6 weeks only, but not at 3, 6 and 9 months. Adding intranasal steroids added no benefit.

Tympanostomy tubes may be considered for children with persistent or recurrent effusion, especially if there is evidence of language delay. Insertion produces a 62% relative decrease in effusion prevalence and an absolute decrease of 128 effusion days per child during the next year. Hearing is improved 6 to 12 dB while tubes are patent. However, up to 50% children will redevelop effusion after tube extrusion. The magnitude of hearing benefit is greatest at 3 months, but drops to 4 dB at 6 to 9 months. Tympanostomy tube insertion with or without adenoidectomy effectively prevents recurrent acute otitis media in children less than 2 years old.

Overall, the insertion of tympanostomy tubes has not been shown to improve language acquistion, cognitive development, or behavioral measures. A study randomizing children to immediate insertion of tubes after at least 90 days of effusion or delayed insertion for 6 to 9 months found no long-term benefit of more aggressive treatment. Patients were followed for as long as 9 years and there were no difference in language development or other clinical outcomes.

Adenoidectomy plus myringotomy produces similar benefits as tympanostomy tubes for children 4 years and older. The added risk of adenoidectomy outweights benefit for children 3 years or older without prior tubes. Among children with prior tubes and effusion recurrence, adenoidectomy confers a 50% reduction in need for further surgery. About 8 adenoidectomies need to be performed to avoid 1 tympanostomy tube reinsertion.

In children aged 3 to 7 years with bilateral CSOM for at least 3 months duration the insertion of tympanostomy tubes in association with adenoidectomy provides no additional bennefit to adenoidectomy in association with myringotomy alone in terms of hearing loss or acute otitis media occurrences at 1 year.
A meta-analysis suggests that primary adenoidectomy plus tympanostomy tube placement may be superior to only tympanostomy tube placement in children greater than four years od age with CSOM.

In an RCT of children with persistent or recurrent otitis or bilateral chronic effusion randomized to adenoidectomy, adenotonsillectomy, or no surgery, there was no important difference between groups in clinical benefit. In children over 3.5 years with persistent bilateral CSOM and hearing loss of greater than or equal to 20 dB in the better ear for three months duration receiving adjuvant adenoidectomy along with tympanostomy tube insertion the need for re-insertion of tympanostomy tubes decreased from 33% to 15% at 18 months.

Evidence is sparse regarding prevention and treatment of otorrhea. Authors of a systematic review conclude from two studies that there is no significant benefit to use of ear plugs for surface swimming, and that topical antibiotics are more effective than oral antibiotics for tympanostomy otorrhea.

Nasal balloon autoinflation (using an "Otovent" device) has been shown in a primary care trial with 320 children to improve ear-related quality of life and increase the likelihihood of a normal tympanogram at 3 months (49% vs. 38%, NNT = 9, p < 0.05). It involves having the child block one nostril while blowing into a nosel attached to a balloon. A video illustrating its use can be found here.
Up to 90% of residual CSOM following acute otitis media will resolve spontaneously by 3 months. B
About 75% to 90% residual CSOM resolves spontaneously following an episode of acute otitis media.
CSOM will resolve in 3 months in about 55% of children whose tympanogram changes from a Type-B to any other curve (improvement has occurred).

About 25% of newly detected CSOM of unknown duration will resolve in children between the ages of 2 and 4 years [resolution defined as a change in tympanogram from Type-B to Type-A/C1 (peak pressure >200 daPa)]. Resolution rates of newly detected CSOM of unknown duration are 22% by 1 month, 28% by 3 months, 42% by 6 months, and 56% by 9 months. CSOM persisting in both ears beyond 3 months resolves spontaneously approximately 20% within 3 months, 25% after 6 months, and only 30% beyond 1 year.
Resolution rates may be higher for infants and young children when the effusion duration is shorter.
Many episodes of CSOM resolve within 3 months with 30% to 40% experiencing recurrence and 5% to 10% having episodes lasting 1 year or longer.
Hearing loss may result in problems with school performance, balance problems or delayed gross motor development, and delayed speech or language development.

Children at greatest risk for these delays have permanent hearing loss independent of CSOM, speech and language delays or disorders, autism spectrum disorder and other pervasive developmental disorders, craniofacial disorders manifested with cognitive, speech, and language delays, uncorrectable visual loss, cleft palate, and developmental delays.

Among patients receiving tympanostomy tubes the risk factors for reoccurrence of significant disease within 12 months of the tympanostomy tube becoming nonfunctional are a low dilatory efficiency of eustachian tube, shorter period of tympanostomy tube patency, male gender, and of non-white race.
At risk children with unilateral or bilateral CSOM reflected by a Type B tympanogram or effusion persistence longer than 3 months may benefit from tympanostomy tube insertion.
If hearing loss is present, the following communication techniques are beneficial:
Be within 3 ft of child when speaking to him.
Turn off competing background audio signals (radio and television).
Face child and speak slowly with a raised volume and enunciate clearly.
Read to or with child and explain pictures asking questions.
Repeat communications to child if felt to be misunderstood.
Assign seating in classrooms close to teacher.
Consider using a frequency modulated personal or sound-field amplification system in classrooms.

CSOM in adults may be related to previous middle ear surgery in the contralateral ear, a history of middle ear disease in childhood, chronic nasal symptoms of obstruction and nasal fullness, cigarette smoking, gastroesophageal reflux (pepsinogen has been found in middle ear fluid), and a family history of middle ear disease.
Any disease entity that produces edema about the eustachian tube orifice in the posterior nasopharynx, such as an upper respiratory infection or nasopharyngeal tumor may produce CSOM.

cell.label: CSOM confirmed by tympanometry. Risk for hearing loss (craniofacial deformities, developmental delays)?
Audiometric evaluation (500, 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz). Greater than 20 dB loss in any frequency?
21-39 is mild loss, ≥40 is moderate loss. Order comprehensive audiologic evaluation. Greater than 20 dB average hearing loss pure tone?

Language testing and otolaryngolic referral. Consider tympanostomy tubes if chronic SOM >3 months or recurrent or persistent chronic SOM. Consider adenoidectomy if nasal obstruction or chronic adenoiditis.
Optimize learning environment. Repeat audiometry in 3-6 months if chronic SOM persists.
